lead: The weekday readings speak of mercy and of signs. Paul asks the Corinthians to forgive a member who has hurt the community, so that he is not overwhelmed by sorrow and Satan gains nothing. In Matthew, Jesus refuses a sign on demand and points to the sign of Jonah: his own death and resurrection, and a call to repent. Today the Church also keeps the memory of St Irenaeus of Lyons, bishop, whose name means “peace”, and offers readings for him: the high priest who bears Israel’s names on his heart, the priest whose lips guard knowledge, the apostolic teaching handed on to Timothy, and the Spirit who reminds the Church of all that Jesus said. Irenaeus guarded that teaching against error and worked for peace in the Church.

set: Paul had made a painful visit to Corinth, during which someone seems to have wronged or openly defied him, and he then wrote a letter “with many tears” (2:4). The community responded and disciplined the offender. Now Paul says the punishment is enough. Older interpreters, among them several Fathers, thought this was the man of 1 Corinthians 5; many scholars today think rather of someone who opposed Paul during that visit. Either way, the point is the same: discipline must lead to healing.
str: vv. 5–6: the offender hurt the whole community; the punishment by the majority is enough.
vv. 7–8: now forgive and console him; reaffirm your love.
vv. 9–11: Paul forgives with them, before Christ, so that Satan may not take advantage.
kw: From charis, grace: to forgive is to give freely what is not deserved, as God has done for us in Christ.
The same root as Paraclete. The community must not only stop punishing; it must comfort and restore.
Literally “in the face of Christ”. The Latin Vulgate rendered it in persona Christi, words that later theology used for the priest who acts in the person of Christ.
vv: so now instead you should forgive and console him, so that he may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Correction that never ends can crush a person. The goal of discipline is to bring the sinner home.
So I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.
Forgiveness is not only a decision in the heart; it must be shown in a public act of welcome.
And we do this so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
Satan can use a community’s harshness as easily as its laxity. An unforgiving Church plays into his hands.
ch: The Catechism teaches that reconciliation with the Church is inseparable from reconciliation with God: whomever the Church receives anew into her communion, God will welcome back into his (CCC 1445). This passage shows that pattern in the first generation: the community corrects, then forgives and restores, and the apostle forgives with it. The Church has always held that the purpose of penance is healing and return, not shame.

set: Jesus has healed a man who was blind and mute, and some have said he casts out demons by Beelzebul (12:22–24). Now some scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, some proof from heaven that will settle the question. Jesus has already given many signs; what they ask for is a sign that will force belief, on their terms.
str: v. 38: the request: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.”
vv. 39–40: no sign but the sign of Jonah: three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
vv. 41–42: the Ninevites and the queen of the South will rise in judgment; something greater is here.
kw: In the Gospels a sign points beyond itself to God’s action. Jesus refuses signs that are demanded to test him (16:1–4).
The word in the Greek Old Testament for the “large fish” of Jonah 1:17. The point is not the kind of animal but God’s rescue from death.
The Greek is neuter: “something more”. Not only a greater prophet or king is here, but the Kingdom itself, present in Jesus.
vv: For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster, so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.
In Jewish reckoning part of a day could count as a day, so Friday afternoon to Sunday morning fits “three days”. The sign is the Resurrection.
because they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
Pagan Nineveh repented at the word of a reluctant prophet. The warning is to every hearer who has the Gospel and does not turn.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him, but that they are not meant to satisfy curiosity or a desire for magic, and that in spite of his evident miracles some reject him (CCC 548). The Church has always read the sign of Jonah as the Lord’s burial and Resurrection (CCC 994 names the sign of Jonah among the Lord’s announcements of his Resurrection). “This generation” in Matthew is the generation that refuses to believe, in any age; it is not a judgment on the Jewish people, and the first to believe in the Risen Lord were themselves Jews (Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: On his heart before the Lord
set: Exodus 28 describes the vestments of Aaron, the high priest. Over his heart he wore the breastpiece, set with twelve precious stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes (28:15–21). Inside it were kept the Urim and Thummim, sacred lots used to seek God’s decision.
str: v. 28: the breastpiece fastened to the ephod with a blue cord, so that it never comes loose.
v. 29: Aaron bears the names of Israel on his heart as a continual remembrance before the Lord.
v. 30: the Urim and Thummim on his heart: he bears the judgment of Israel before the Lord continually.
kw: A square pouch of woven cloth worn on the chest. It is called “of judgment” because through it God’s decision was sought for the people.
Sacred lots whose exact form is unknown. The words are often explained as “lights and perfections”. They showed that the priest does not decide by himself but seeks God’s will.
vv: So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart when he goes into the holy place, for a continual remembrance before the Lord.
The priest enters God’s presence carrying the people on his heart. A shepherd remembers his flock by name when he prays.
thus Aaron shall bear the judgment of the Israelites on his heart before the Lord continually.
“Continually” is said twice. Intercession is not occasional; it is the shape of a priest’s life.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews sees all the priesthood of Aaron fulfilled in Christ, the high priest who “always lives to make intercession” for those who approach God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The Catechism teaches that everything the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured finds its fulfilment in Christ, the one mediator (CCC 1544). A bishop like Irenaeus shares in that priesthood and carries his people on his heart.

r.h: The lips of a priest should guard knowledge
set: Malachi preached after the return from exile, in the fifth century before Christ, when the Temple had been rebuilt but worship had grown careless. The priests offered blemished animals and taught falsely (1:6–14; 2:8). God reminds them of his covenant with Levi, the ancestor of the priestly tribe, as a picture of what a priest should be.
str: v. 4: the command is given so that the covenant with Levi may stand.
vv. 5–6: a covenant of life and peace; Levi revered God, taught truly and turned many from sin.
v. 7: the priest’s lips guard knowledge; he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts.
kw: Here not the written Law alone but the teaching the priest gives the people. True instruction was “in his mouth”.
The same word as the prophet’s name, Malachi, “my messenger”. The priest who teaches truly speaks for God.
vv: True instruction was in his mouth, and no wrong was found on his lips. He walked with me in integrity and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity.
Teaching and life go together. Levi’s words could turn others because his own walk was upright.
For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts.
The priest is a guardian of truth he did not invent. People have a right to sound teaching.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the first task of priests, as co-workers of the bishops, is to proclaim the Gospel of God to all (Presbyterorum Ordinis 4), and that bishops are authentic teachers of the faith (Lumen Gentium 25). Irenaeus lived this verse: he wrote to protect his people from teachings that twisted the Scriptures, setting out the faith received from the apostles.

r.h: Continue in what you have learned
set: The letter presents itself as Paul’s last testament to Timothy, written from prison as his death draws near (4:6). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Paul’s name, while others hold it is Paul’s own; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way. Timothy had learned the faith from his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (1:5) and from Paul himself.
str: v. 14: continue in what you have learned, knowing from whom you learned it.
v. 15: from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which lead to salvation through faith in Christ.
vv. 16–17: all scripture is inspired by God and useful for teaching, reproof, correction and training.
kw: Literally “God-breathed”. The Scriptures come from the breath, the Spirit, of God, while being truly written by human authors.
The word for the upbringing of a child. Scripture forms a person over a lifetime, not only in moments of study.
vv: But as for you, continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it
Faith is received from trustworthy people. Knowing from whom we learned is part of knowing that it is true.
All scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness
At first “scripture” meant what we call the Old Testament. The Church, guided by the Spirit, recognized the apostolic writings with it as one Bible.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse in teaching that the books of Scripture, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, have God as their author, and teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wanted put into writing for our salvation (Dei Verbum 11; CCC 105–107). Irenaeus was a living example of verse 14: as a boy in Asia Minor he heard St Polycarp, who had known the apostle John, and he could say from whom he had learned (in substance, Eusebius, Church History 5.20).

set: At the Last Supper Jesus prepares his disciples for his departure. He promises the Advocate, gives them his peace, and tells them that his going to the Father is reason for joy. The hour of the Passion is near: “the ruler of this world is coming.”
str: v. 26: the Advocate, sent by the Father in my name, will teach you and remind you.
v. 27: my peace I give you, not as the world gives.
vv. 28–29: rejoice that I go to the Father; I tell you before it happens.
v. 30: the ruler of this world is coming; he has no power over me.
kw: One called to stand beside another, to defend, comfort and guide. The Spirit continues Jesus’ own presence with the disciples.
The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel but makes the Church remember and understand what Jesus said.
vv: But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.
Here is the root of the Church’s living Tradition: the Spirit keeps Jesus’ words alive and leads the Church into their depth.
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives.
The world’s peace depends on the absence of trouble. Christ’s peace remains even in the hour of the Cross.
If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.

The Church reads this in the light of the faith that the Son is equal to the Father. St Augustine explains it of the Son in the form of a servant he took for our sake (in substance, Tractates on John); other Fathers read it of the Father as the source from whom the Son is eternally begotten.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, recalls to the Church all that Christ said and guides her into all truth (CCC 243, 729). St Irenaeus wrote that where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God, and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church and every grace (in substance, Against Heresies 3.24.1). He also called the Son and the Spirit the “two hands” of the Father, by which God forms and saves the human person (in substance, Against Heresies 4, preface; 5.6.1).

qa: He was born in Asia Minor, probably around AD 130–140, and as a youth heard St Polycarp of Smyrna, a disciple of the apostle John. He became a priest at Lyons in Gaul, and after the bishop Pothinus died in the persecution of 177, he succeeded him. His great work, Against Heresies, defended the faith against the Gnostics by appealing to the Scriptures and to the teaching handed down by the bishops in succession from the apostles. When Pope Victor threatened to cut off the Churches of Asia over the date of Easter, Irenaeus urged peace, living up to his name (Eusebius, Church History 5.24). He died around AD 200; later tradition honours him as a martyr, though early sources are silent. In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, with the title “Doctor of Unity”.
rite: Irenaeus came from the East and served in the West; he belongs to the whole Church. For Syro-Malabar Catholics, who treasure an apostolic faith received from Mar Thoma Shleeha and kept through the centuries, his teaching is close to home: the faith is known by its apostolic roots and kept in communion. His famous saying, that the glory of God is the human person fully alive (in substance, Against Heresies 4.20.7), is a fitting prayer for every family.
study: Paul asks the Corinthians to forgive and console a man who had hurt them. Is there someone in my family or parish whom I need to welcome back?
Irenaeus could say from whom he had learned the faith. Who handed the faith on to me, and to whom am I handing it on?
